chunks: Trade-offs of sharper square-wave edges. The question: What are the tradeoffs of sharper edges on a square wave?
A sharper edge is a faster jump from low to high. Sharper edges give more timing room and less sensitivity to noise.
They also create more high-frequency energy, which causes interference, ringing and supply noise.
So you pick the slowest edge that still meets your timing, not the fastest edge the chip can make.
Think of driving a car. Hard acceleration and hard braking get you there sooner, but the ride is rough, the engine is loud, and the car behind you has to react.
Smooth driving is calmer for everyone but takes longer. A signal edge works the same way: speed buys time, and costs noise for the neighbors.
The best driver goes only as fast as the trip actually requires.
Timing error from a fixed voltage noise is directly proportional to rise time. Slowing the edge 5 times makes the jitter 5 times worse for the same noise.
That matters most when the unit interval is short, which is one reason fast links cannot afford slow edges.
Edge / rise time: the switch from low to high. A shorter rise time means a sharper edge.
Timing margin: spare time between when data is steady and when the receiving chip needs it. Ringing: wobbles after an edge, like a bell still humming ("Ringing").
Crosstalk: a signal leaking into a neighboring wire ("Crosstalk"). EMI: unwanted radio-frequency energy that a circuit gives off or picks up.
Say data moves at 1 Gb/s, so each bit lasts 1 nanoseconds. An edge that takes 100 picoseconds uses 10% of the bit, leaving 90% as steady time for the receiver to read.
An edge that takes 400 picoseconds uses 40%, leaving only 60%. The faster edge wins on timing. The cost shows up in the high frequencies.
Above a certain frequency (the "knee", set by the edge speed), a 10 times faster edge puts 10 times more voltage into the high-frequency content (engineers call that 20 decibels more).
More energy there means more crosstalk, EMI and ringing. That is the whole idea: one knob, edge speed, helps timing and hurts noise.
"Sharper edges buy timing margin, less jitter from noise because jitter is noise over slew rate, and lower switching loss in power stages.

The price is more high-frequency content: more EMI, more crosstalk, more ground bounce and supply droop, and reflections and ringing from every discontinuity, so you need controlled impedance, termination and a tighter layout.
I try to use the slowest edge that still meets timing, using slew-rate control or a series resistor."
